brandRevenue.title: Net sales by brand
brandRevenue.content:
Tapestry runs three (now two) distinct brands as separate reportable segments: Coach, Kate Spade and, through 4 August 2025, Stuart Weitzman (sold to Caleres).

For Tapestry: Coach is resurging -- net sales +23.5% in FY2026 and +16.1% in Q1 FY2027 -- while Kate Spade has been shrinking for several years and took an $854.8m goodwill/brand impairment in FY2025. The blended Revenue line hides both moves.

What to watch:

  • Whether Coach's growth is handbags/leather-goods-led or driven by a weaker dollar and price increases
  • Kate Spade's sales trend stabilising versus still declining
  • Stuart Weitzman's series stops after the FY2026 stub period -- it is not a reporting gap

brandOperatingMargin.title: Operating margin by brand
brandOperatingMargin.content:
Segment operating income divided by segment net sales for each brand -- the profitability each brand delivers before corporate overhead allocation.

For Tapestry: Kate Spade swung to an operating loss in FY2025 on the impairment and has stayed there on a shrinking revenue base, while Coach's margin has held in the mid-to-high 20s%. The brand mix, not just the blended OperatingMargin column, is the story behind Tapestry's consolidated margin trend.

What to watch:

  • Whether Kate Spade returns to positive operating income or management repositions/divests it, as it did Stuart Weitzman
  • Coach's margin trend as the growth driver funding the group

geoRevenue.title: Revenue by geography
geoRevenue.content:
Net sales split between North America, Greater China, Other Asia and the rest of the world (Europe, Latin America, etc. -- Tapestry's "Other" bucket).

For Tapestry: North America is still the large majority of sales, but Greater China is the swing factor for the Coach growth story and the most macro-sensitive region given consumer demand and tariff exposure.

What to watch:

  • Greater China growth or contraction relative to North America
  • Whether Other Asia (Japan, Korea, SE Asia) is picking up share China loses, or moving together with it

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Tapestry, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Tapestry, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Tapestry, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Tapestry, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Tapestry, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Tapestry, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Tapestry, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Tapestry, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Tapestry, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Tapestry, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
